models.collectorNote: Airflyte cars are the design icons; the 1957 V8 cars are the rarest. Nash's overhead-valve engineering is durable, neglect, not design, kills them.

generations.name: Ambassador Eight
generations.note: The twin-ignition overhead-valve eight was Nash's pride: two spark plugs per cylinder in the 1930s. War stopped production in 1942; the six-cylinder Ambassador returned for 1946–48.

generations.name: Ambassador Airflyte / V8
generations.note: The 1949 Airflyte brought the enclosed-wheel 'bathtub' body and seats that folded into a bed. A V8 arrived in 1956; the 1957 cars, restyled with stacked quad headlamps, were the last Nash-badged Ambassadors.

models.intro: Nash's flagship for a quarter century: overhead-valve engines when rivals ran flatheads, unit construction, reclining seats, and the bathtub Airflyte styling that defined post-war Nash. The nameplate outlived the company, AMC kept building Ambassadors after Nash itself was gone.

models.collectorNote: Convertibles and Country Club hardtops lead; these were the best-selling Ramblers and the survivors are plentiful enough that condition decides price.

generations.name: Rambler (Nash)
generations.note: Launched as a convertible, the body engineering shortcut that let the unit body stay rigid, then a wagon and hardtop. The L-head six was modest; the idea was not.

models.intro: The car that started the American compact era: George Romney's bet that a smaller, cheaper, well-equipped Nash could beat the Big Three's bulk. It could. The Rambler name went on to anchor AMC, and this little Airflyte convertible is where it began.

models.collectorNote: Cheerful, simple and fully supported by the Metropolitan clubs and parts network; rust in the sills and A-posts is the whole inspection.

generations.name: Metropolitan 1200 / 1500
generations.note: Series I cars used Austin's 1.2-litre A40 engine at 42 hp; the 1.5-litre B-series from 1956 gave 52–55 hp. About 95,000 were built, most for North America.

models.intro: An American idea built in England: Nash commissioned Austin to build its tiny Metropolitan in Birmingham, sold it as a Nash and then a Hudson, and proved a market for small cars existed a decade before Detroit admitted it. Two-tone paint and a continental spare were standard charm.

models.collectorNote: Genuinely rare and historically first; Pininfarina cars carry the premium. Panelcraft and Farina body provenance should be documented car by car.

generations.name: Nash-Healey roadster / Le Mans coupé
generations.note: Just 506 cars were built. The 1952 redesign by Pinin Farina added the coupé and the larger 4.1-litre 'Le Mans' dual-carburettor engine.

models.intro: America's first post-war sports car beat the Corvette to market: Donald Healey's chassis, Nash's overhead-valve six, and from 1952 a Pininfarina body built in Turin. A Nash-Healey finished third overall at Le Mans in 1952, the marque's finest hour, in a car almost nobody bought.
